title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator to evaluate whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline improves operational correctness relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM on intent→configuration tasks. The confirmatory paired design used N=300 tasks (75 per intent cluster), a shared‑initial candidate per task, and a guarded repair budget ≤1 call/task. Declared model: gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Execution accounting: planned 600 episodes, completed 600, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d. Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.996667), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered target effect (0.10) was not supported: a near‑ceiling baseline and minimal repair engagement (repair invoked exactly once) rendered the preregistered detectable effect unattainable. We explain this arithmetic ceiling, report all archived artifacts enabling deterministic inspection (including how to locate the single repair provider trace in execution/raw_results.jsonl), state which preregistered secondary analyses were not executed, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for future confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks including intent→configuration translation, change planning, and automated remediation. Prior work shows LLMs can draft plausible device commands but often produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; combining generation with deterministic verification and localized repair (generate–validate–repair, GVR) is a commonly proposed mitigation. Yet the community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that pair explicit operational intents with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration for confirmatory inference. To address this, we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1: (1) a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) a stateless snapshot validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) that enforces required sequences and workflow policies, and (3) a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass generator using a shared‑initial candidate design. The research question (preregistered) was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does the GVR pipeline materially increase per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and targeted studies document active interest in LLMs for network management and emphasize core operational challenges—hallucination, prompt injection, verifier integration, and the need for reproducible evaluation [https://openalex.org/W4406137434; https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical prototypes show LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193; 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Tool‑assisted, generate–validate–repair approaches can improve final correctness in focused demonstrations, though those results are dataset‑specific and limited in scale [https://openalex.org/W4404652946]. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompting motivate guarded architectures with deterministic checks prior to device changes [https://openalex.org/W4405181600; https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our contribution is an artifact‑anchored, preregistered confirmatory run that ties a deterministic validator to an automated repair trigger under a narrowly specified budget and that releases the archived traces required for deterministic auditing.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and confirmatory hypothesis. We preregistered the design (study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1; preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration fixed task generation, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness treatment, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and a conservative repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate). The design used a shared initial candidate per task: that same generated candidate served as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline’s initial input; guarded repairs could only be invoked on validator failure and were limited to a single automated repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑initial pairing isolates repair value from multi‑sample selection or reranking effects.
sections.results: Execution summary and provider accounting. The run completed successfully: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call). The authoritative provider traces are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Deterministic reconciliation shows stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1} (deterministic_reconciliation.json in the artifact bundle).
sections.discussion: Confirmatory outcomes and arithmetic ceiling. The primary confirmatory counts were: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (0.9966667), guarded_success_count = 300/300 (1.0); contingency table n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0 because the test depends only on discordant pairs (n10 and n01); with n10 = 1 and n01 = 0 the exact two‑sided p reported by the preregistered executor equals 1.0. This p‑value is numerically correct but uninformative under the observed ceiling (very few discordant pairs); the paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01] provides a more practically interpretable uncertainty bound. The preregistered target effect (0.10 absolute increase) was arithmetically unattainable given the marginal totals: the maximal possible paired gain given baseline margin ≈0.997 is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed increment).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and performed a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline against a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported; the null outcome is explained by a ceiling baseline and effectively inert repair engagement (repair invoked exactly once). We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, provider traces, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable community reuse and to support follow‑on confirmatory designs with higher baseline difficulty, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, or stateful emulation validators that can expose measurable repair benefits.

disclosure_statement: This study followed the sealed preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765) archived with the execution bundle. Declared model and generation settings (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) were: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 implemented the shared initial generation (one shared call per task) and the guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline with maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implementing scoring rule "full_intent_constraint_validation"; per‑task scorer outputs and validator traces are archived under execution/scoring/*.json (representative examples included). Preregistered analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar and paired bootstrap CI; bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Execution accounting (authoritative): planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call). Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} (deterministic_reconciliation.json). The authoritative provider traces are in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). The single repair provider trace and the corresponding discordant episode identifier are recorded inside execution/raw_results.jsonl; auditors can deterministically locate this entry by filtering execution/raw_results.jsonl for the single record whose stage field equals "repair" (there is exactly one such record in execution/raw_results.jsonl, as evidenced by stage_counts above). That record contains the pair_id field and the full provider_call trace needed to reproduce the repair invocation. Initial master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy: a human Research Director selected the topic family and provided pre‑lock constraints and the initial master prompt; after the autonomy lock the autonomous pipeline performed literature synthesis, study selection, sealed preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29…).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifact that contains the single repair provider trace and the discordant episode identifier is present in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and can be deterministically retrieved by filtering that file for the single record with stage == "repair".
